source.note: Structured, paraphrased knowledge derived from the Chess.com cheat sheet and linked concept pages; no opening-book moves or engine evaluations are included.

objective: Checkmate the opponent while keeping your own king safe and obeying all legal-move constraints.
turns: Players alternate one legal move at a time.

king: Moves one square in any direction to a legal square.
The king may not move into check or remain in check.
queen: Moves any unobstructed distance horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.
rook: Moves any unobstructed distance horizontally or vertically.
knight: Moves in an L shape: two squares on one axis and one on the other.
pawn: Moves one square forward into an empty square.
From its starting rank may move two squares forward if both squares are empty.
White pawns move toward rank 8; Black pawns move toward rank 1.

captures: A normal capture moves onto a square occupied by an enemy piece and removes that piece.
A piece may not move onto a friendly piece.
check: A king is in check when attacked by an enemy piece.
A move is illegal if it leaves the moving side's king in check.
A checked player must make a move that removes the check.
checkmate: Checkmate occurs when the king is in check and no legal escape exists.
Delivering checkmate ends the game immediately and wins regardless of material balance.
stalemate: No legal move while not in check is stalemate and is a draw.
castling: Castling moves the king two squares toward a rook and moves that rook across the king.
Castling requires that the king and chosen rook have not moved and that squares between them are empty.
The king may not castle while in check, through an attacked square, or into check.
Castling is strategically useful because it improves king safety and activates a rook.
en_passant: A pawn may capture an adjacent enemy pawn immediately after that pawn advances two squares, as if it had advanced one square.
The opportunity exists only on the immediately following move.
promotion: A pawn reaching the final rank must promote to a queen, rook, bishop, or knight.
draws: Threefold repetition may be claimed when the same position with equivalent move rights recurs three times.
The fifty-move rule may be claimed after fifty moves by each side without a pawn move or capture.
Insufficient mating material produces a draw.
Players may agree to a draw.
termination: Applicable draw conditions end the game as a draw.

development: Develop pieces so they participate actively rather than remaining blocked on their starting squares.
Prefer useful development that improves coordination and future options.
center_control: Control central squares because central influence increases mobility and access to both sides of the board.
Moves that occupy or attack the center can improve piece activity.
king_safety: Protect the king; an exposed king can outweigh material advantages.
Moving the king away from the center and maintaining protective pawn cover is often desirable.
material: Track the relative value and quantity of pieces to detect material advantages or losses.
Material advantage is useful but may be outweighed by checkmate threats or strong activity.
piece_activity: Active pieces influence useful squares, attack targets, defend allies, and create threats.
A position with more active pieces can compensate for some material deficit.
mobility: More safe and useful move options generally increase flexibility and attacking or defensive potential.
pawn_structure: Pawn placement shapes long-term strengths, weaknesses, open lines, and available plans.
Avoid creating unnecessary structural weaknesses unless compensated by another advantage.
space: A space advantage provides more room for pieces to maneuver.
Restricting the opponent's useful squares can reduce their activity.

forcing_play: Tactical opportunities are short-term sequences that can force material gain or checkmate.
Checks, captures, and direct threats deserve special examination because they constrain replies.
pin: A pinned piece is constrained because moving it would expose a more valuable piece, critical square, or king.
skewer: A skewer attacks a valuable piece first so that, after it moves, a less valuable piece behind it can be captured.
fork: A fork occurs when one piece attacks two or more valuable targets at the same time.
discovered_attack: A discovered attack occurs when one piece moves away and reveals an attack by another piece.
tactical_priority: A sound forcing tactic that wins decisive material or checkmates can take precedence over slower strategic improvements.

reasoning_guidance: For each legal move, consider whether it develops a piece, controls the center, improves king safety, preserves or wins material, increases activity or mobility, improves space, or avoids pawn weaknesses.
Also test each candidate for immediate tactical consequences: checks, captures, threats, pins, skewers, forks, and discovered attacks.
Prefer moves whose predicted consequences advance the objective while surviving the opponent's strongest plausible reply.
Treat strategic and tactical principles as defeasible guidance, not immutable facts; concrete tactical evidence can override a general heuristic.

notation.test_move_format: UCI coordinate notation such as e2e4 or e7e8q
notation.note: Notation is representation only and does not alter the rules.
